Section 01

Dataset Overview & Game Distribution

The dataset comprises 20,058 chess games from Lichess.org. Of these, 16,155 (80.5%) were rated and 3,903 (19.5%) were casual. Among all games, 10,001 were won by White, 9,107 by Black, and 950 ended in a draw. The decisive-game split gives White a 52.3% win rate vs. Black's 47.7%.

Key observation: Resignation is the dominant game-ending mode at 55.6% of all games, followed by checkmate at 31.5%. Only 8.4% of games end by timeout, and 4.5% end in draws.
Section 02

White vs. Black: The First-Move Advantage

White wins 52.3% of decisive games — a 2.3 percentage-point advantage over the theoretical 50% baseline. This edge persists across virtually all rating brackets and time controls, though its magnitude shifts considerably.

Centerpiece finding: White's advantage is most pronounced in Classical time controls among lower-rated players, where the first-move advantage compounds with deeper calculation ability. In Bullet, the edge narrows as clock management dominates over positional advantages. The 2.3-point White advantage is consistent but not uniform — it is a gradient, not a constant.
Section 03

Rating Dynamics and Their Impact on Outcomes

The average player rating is 1593, with a standard deviation of 263. Rating differential is the single strongest predictor of game outcome: the Pearson correlation between absolute rating difference and higher-rated-player victory is 0.248.

Rating Differential Impact: Binned Analysis

How does the higher-rated player's win probability shift as the rating gap widens? The table and chart below show a monotonic relationship — every 100-point increment in rating difference adds roughly 8-12 percentage points to the stronger player's win probability.

Game Length by Rating Tier

Rating dynamics insight: A 200-point rating gap gives the stronger player approximately a 76% chance of winning — a decisive but not insurmountable edge. At 500+ point gaps, the win probability exceeds 88%. Higher-rated players also tend to play longer games (more turns), suggesting deeper engagement and fewer early blunders.

Section 06

Key Findings and Strategic Takeaways

The following findings synthesize the most impactful patterns discovered across all analyses. Each is grounded in the data and immediately actionable for players, coaches, and platform analysts.

1. White's Edge is Real but Modest

White wins 52.3% of decisive games — a 2.3-point advantage. This is statistically meaningful but far from decisive. Black players should not feel disadvantaged at the board; the edge is smaller than a single rating bracket's typical variation.

2. Time Pressure Amplifies First-Move Advantage

White's advantage grows in Classical time controls and shrinks in Bullet. When players have time to calculate, White's initial position matters more. Under severe time pressure, clock management overwhelms positional factors.

3. Rating Gap is the Dominant Predictor

A 0.25 correlation between rating differential and outcome makes it the strongest single predictor. A 200-point gap yields ~76% win probability for the stronger player. A 500+ point gap makes upsets rare but not impossible.

4. Resignation Dominates, Checkmate is Rare

56% of games end by resignation vs. only 32% by checkmate. Players reliably recognize lost positions — games rarely need to reach mate. Timeout accounts for 8%, concentrated in Bullet.

5. Opening Choice Matters Less Than Execution

Among top 15 openings, White win rates span only a ~25-point range. No opening eliminates White's advantage, and only a handful see Black equal or exceed White's win rate. Opening preparation helps, but post-opening play determines outcomes.

6. Higher Ratings = Longer Games

Stronger players play more turns per game — from ~48 turns at the lowest tier to ~68 at the highest. This reflects better defensive technique, fewer early blunders, and the ability to convert small advantages over longer sequences.
